youtube_title: RGV Development Brief: Industrial Parks, a $164M Water Bet & the Treaty Risk | Nov 13, 2026

scenes.headline:
2 opportunities.
1 risk to watch.
scenes.narration: This is RGV News, your brief on the developments shaping the Rio Grande Valley, and what they mean if you build, buy, or invest here. Today: two opportunities, and one risk you should be watching.

scenes.headline: Industrial growth near the Anzalduas bridge
scenes.narration: First, industrial land in the Mission and McAllen corridor.

scenes.label: Sharyland Business Park · Mission
scenes.caption:
Killam Development master plan, purchased Dec 2019.
Park sits under a mile from the Anzalduas International Bridge.
scenes.narration: Killam Development's Sharyland Business Park sits less than a mile from the Anzalduas International Bridge. It's part of a thirty-four hundred acre master plan that Killam bought in late 2019, spanning Mission and McAllen.

scenes.label: Phase one → planned build-out
scenes.caption:
Ground broken May 2022 · manufacturing, logistics, cold storage
~$8M in infrastructure already invested (per Killam)
scenes.narration: Phase one broke ground in May 2022 on a hundred and seventy-five acres, aimed at manufacturing, logistics, and cold storage. Plans call for the park to grow to as much as one thousand acres, and Killam reports about eight million dollars already invested in infrastructure.

scenes.label: City of McAllen · industrial park
scenes.caption:
Federal grant reported in July 2026
(U.S. Economic Development Administration)
scenes.narration: Next door, the City of McAllen has received a six million dollar federal grant for its own industrial park project, reported this summer as coming from the U.S. Economic Development Administration.

scenes.headline: Why it matters
bullets: Border-adjacent industrial jobs pull demand for workforce housing
Retail and services follow the corridors that feed them
Watch where employers actually sign leases
scenes.narration: Why it matters: industrial jobs near a border crossing tend to pull demand for workforce housing, retail, and services along the corridors that feed them. If you're looking at land or entry-level housing in western Hidalgo County, watch where these employers actually sign leases.

scenes.headline: A $164 million bet on the Valley's water system
scenes.narration: Second: a hundred and sixty-four million dollar push to modernize how the Valley moves its water.

scenes.label: Proposed funding · subject to board approvals
scenes.narration: The North American Development Bank proposed up to seventy-six million dollars in financing for twelve Lower Rio Grande Valley irrigation districts, with the Texas Water Development Board expected to add nearly seventy million in grants. Both pieces were announced subject to board approval.

scenes.label: Estimated water saved
scenes.caption:
Canal lining and conversion to pipe
Cameron · Hidalgo · Starr · Willacy counties
scenes.narration: The money targets canal lining and converting open canals to pipe, cutting the water lost in transit. Reported estimates put the savings near forty-four thousand acre-feet a year.

scenes.headline: Why it matters
bullets: Water is the quiet constraint behind every new subdivision
Efficiency doesn't create water, but it stretches supply
Track final approvals from NADBank and TWDB
scenes.narration: For developers, water is the quiet constraint behind every new subdivision. More efficient delivery doesn't create new water, but it stretches what the region already has. Watch for the final approvals.

scenes.headline: The 1944 Water Treaty shortfall
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the risk.

scenes.label: Mexico's obligation per 5-year cycle
scenes.caption:
≈ 350,000 acre-feet per year on average
Cycle closed Oct 24, 2025: Texas says Mexico fell short
scenes.narration: Under the 1944 Water Treaty, Mexico owes the United States an average of three hundred fifty thousand acre-feet a year, or one point seven five million over each five-year cycle. When the last cycle closed on October twenty-fourth, 2025, Texas officials said Mexico fell short.

scenes.headline: Questions to ask before you underwrite
bullets: How is the city's water supply secured?
How is new growth being permitted?
Are utility costs likely to rise?
scenes.narration: The treaty has no direct penalty for missing a target, and Falcon and Amistad reservoirs have run low in recent years. If you're underwriting a project in the Valley, ask how the city's water supply is secured, how new growth is being permitted, and whether utility costs are likely to rise.
